# Build handover: starting M7

Written 2026-11-04, after M6 merged. This is the resume point for the next coordinator. It covers what to do next,
how to run the work and how to decide. What earlier milestones built is in their results notes
(`docs/build/m0-results.md` to `m6-results.md`), and why things are as they are is in `docs/LOG.md`.

## 1. Where things stand

- M0 to M6 of `docs/11-build-plan.md` are on `main`. The engine now runs an epic of tickets and a project over two
  repositories end to end. Along the way it records findings in a ledger, checks plans and claims with the standard
  validators, and reads and updates GitHub issues. A person's merge into `main` is detected (floor F1: only a person
  merges into a default branch).
- M6's two live runs proved this on the fixtures (`m6-results.md`, "Integration"):
  - an epic of three issue-tracked tickets merged into its parent branch;
  - a project delivered to `feature-flow-example`, then `feature-flow-example-client`, with the product owner's two
    merges detected and `delivery.report` saying `complete`.
- **Nothing awaits the product owner.** LOG 1 to 200 are approved; 148 to 200, M6's judgement calls, on 2026-11-04.
  New judgement calls start at **LOG 201**.
- Only `main` exists on GitHub. No worktrees are open. Both fixtures have only `main`.

## 2. What to do next: M7, people, policy and steering

Read M7 in `docs/11` section 4: what it builds, its done-when and its checks. M6 left three things M7 should take
first, because the live runs showed their cost:

1. **Check produced artifacts at report time, with correction turns** (LOG 176; M6 integration follow-up 2). Today a
   malformed plan or findings report goes back through an intervention or a whole re-run. In M6's live runs, haiku
   planners lost many attempts this way; one ticket planner needed six attempts granted by a person. `docs/01`
   section 5.4 already designs this, so it is overdue rather than new.
2. **A person triages findings** through a decision (LOG 168, 169). Until then an escalated or declined blocking
   finding reaches a person only as an intervention, answered by recovery actions. The actor must be the
   authenticated person (F8).
3. **Recoveries a person needs** (integration follow-ups 3 and 4):
   - re-run a failed branch of a finished parallel step (today `go_to` re-runs the step but not the join, and the run
     ends `incomplete`);
   - aborting a run closes the pull requests it opened.

**Follow-ups that must not be lost**

- **M4 follow-up 12:** the sandbox's network is unrestricted and reaches the Temporal frontend. Fix this before any shared
  deployment (M8 at the latest).
- The rest are in `m6-results.md`, "Consolidated follow-ups". Pick up any M7 touches.

Still deferred: `docs/11` open question 4 (the team deployment's object store and container platform).

## 3. How to run a milestone

M6 ran as M5 did, and it worked: every builder's first independent review came back "changes-required" (integration's:
approve-with-fixes), and every catch was real. Examples:

- a triager agent alone could close a demonstrated bug and merge;
- a planner could mark its own criteria as "owned" and merge with no tests;
- `delivery.report` counted a stale or reverted merge;
- a wait cancelled mid-read used an attempt.

The shape:

1. **Interfaces first** (one worker, on a branch into the milestone branch). The coordinator reviews, then the files
   freeze. M6's took 30 minutes and saved every builder a cross-branch change.
2. **Parallel builders** (M6 had four), each on its own branch and files, with its own LOG range, Temporal port and
   results-note section. Put the shared rules in one file every brief points to
   (M6's, kept in the coordinator's session folder, held: what to read, hard limits, environment, engineering rules,
   LOG and results-note rules, commit trailers and the report headings). Each brief then only says what is that
   worker's own.
3. **Independent review of every pull request**, by a reviewer that gets the code and the design, not the builder's
   report, and must break the code to show the tests catch it. Then a **re-check** by the same reviewer after the
   fixes. M6's re-checks found a second, smaller layer each time (a no-op fix plus a wrong verifier verdict; a route
   lost silently in a merge). For the last small fix round, the coordinator checked the diff and merged.
4. **Integration** on the milestone branch: cross-piece checks, then the live done-when. M6's live runs found 14 more
   seams that no unit or integration test had shown. Budget for several live attempts: the project took seven.
   Integration's own commits get a short independent review too.
5. **Merge commits only.** Delete merged branches locally and on GitHub. Clean up worktrees.

**Working with worker chats** (as before, plus M6's lessons)

- Brief each worker completely; give it a report file with fixed headings, and read reports from that file.
- **Watch report files against a marker, not a snapshot.** A watcher that snapshots the state when it starts misses a
  report written before it starts. Touch a marker file after reading, and wait for report files newer than it (`find -newer`). The machine may also sleep overnight.
- **Merges between parallel builders need care.** Tell each builder when the milestone branch moves. In M6, one
  three-way merge silently made a new step unreachable (a YAML route), and another would have bound a positional
  argument to the wrong new parameter. Re-run the re-drive and integration suites after every merge.
- A builder whose LOG range runs out extends its own latest entries; give integration a spare range.
- **Worker pitfalls:**
  - this machine sets `safe.bareRepository=explicit`; tests using a bare repository need
    `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT=1 GIT_CONFIG_KEY_0=safe.bareRepository GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0=all` in the test environment only;
  - keep stress runs bounded;
  - the hosts ignore SIGTERM when run detached and need SIGKILL.

**Reaching the product owner.** In M6 the product owner answered in this chat. The Slack bot can post (Keychain
`SLACK_BOT_TOKEN`, channel in `~/.ff/config.json`), but reading replies needs the Slack MCP, which may need a fresh
sign-in. Post at milestone transitions and for decisions.

## 4. How to decide

As in `docs/build/handover-2026-11-03-m6.md` section 4: follow `CONTRIBUTING.md`'s development and decision
guidelines, keep the floors pragmatically, a safety rule must not depend on a file the governed party can edit, and
evidence comes only from engine actions. Two principles M6 added, both from reviews:

- **The governed agent alone must not clear what blocks it.** Only an independent step (the verifier after a real fix)
  or a person can close a blocking or demonstrated finding (LOG 168). Route on engine counts, never on an agent's own
  outputs.
- **Acceptance criteria are met only by engine test evidence at the frozen head, or by a person,** never by the
  agent's own classification (LOG 178). An owner that is the run itself counts as unowned.

What counts as major is unchanged. M6's major decisions, both taken by the product owner:

- the GitHub App's Issues permission;
- creating the second fixture repository.

## 5. Access and environment

As in `handover-2026-11-03-m6.md` section 5, with these changes:

| Need | How |
|---|---|
| Fixtures | `ai-feature-flow/feature-flow-example` (the API) and `ai-feature-flow/feature-flow-example-client` (its client, created in M6; one `unit` tier in CI), both public, both with the ruleset `protect-main` (a pull request into `main`). Live runs are approved on both and must leave no references behind. M6's changes stay on both `main`s (product owner) |
| Tracker | GitHub Issues through the App, which has **Issues: read and write** (product owner, 2026-11-04). Agents get no issues scope |
| A live epic or project run | `m6-results.md`, "Integration", and M5's how-to. A project run needs a person to merge each repository's pull request into `main` in order |
